FloralFlair

An online flower shop designed to make discovering and buying bouquets pleasant, simple and visually engaging.

TypeE-commerce website
FocusVisual design, product discovery, navigation
ScreensHome, Shop, Product, About, Contact

Purpose

Flowers are bought for feelings: gifts, weddings, apologies. The site needed to show the product beautifully and then get out of the way so purchase feels easy.

Intended users

Likely users, not researched: gift buyers who want something fresh quickly, people planning events who need custom or larger arrangements, and first-time visitors who need to trust the shop.

What users need

See flowers clearly, compare prices at a glance, understand delivery and returns, and find help if the choice is hard.

Shopping journey shown in the screens

  1. Home: offer and new arrivals
  2. Shop: all 9 products
  3. Product: images, price, Add to Cart
  4. Related products
  5. Contact and FAQs for help

Visual design

Colour: blush-pink backgrounds with black bands and one saturated red for every primary action, so buttons are never in doubt. Type: a serif for headings and product names gives a classic, floral feel; a clean sans for navigation. Imagery: bouquet photos on plain or coloured backdrops keep the product the hero.

Discovery and navigation

A four-link navigation (Home, About, Shop, Contact) with a persistent cart icon. Breadcrumbs and related products on the product page support moving sideways without going back. The footer repeats links, help and contact details.

Responsive considerations

The three-column grids and split sections are built to stack on narrower widths. Mobile layouts are not among the screens supplied, so this is a design intent rather than something shown here.

Retrospective: what I would improve

  • Add category filters and sorting on Shop; with nine products it works, with more it will not.
  • Make the brand consistent: the header says “Flower Shop”, the footer says FloralFlair, and the contact page labels the nav “Sales” instead of “Shop”.
  • Check text contrast on the red buttons (the Submit label is dark on red) and on the grey category labels.
  • Tidy a few text rendering glitches visible in the home screenshot, such as “New Arrival” and the testimonials.
  • Replace placeholder text in the FAQs and sample testimonials before launch.

Key learnings

Shopping UIs get their clarity from repetition: one card pattern, one button colour, one price format. I also learned that trust content (shipping, refunds, FAQs) belongs near the decision, not only in the footer.

MediMantra

A mobile app for wellbeing: guided meditation by need, a customisable timer and simple stretching exercises.

TypeHealthcare and wellbeing mobile app UI
FocusClarity, readability, trust
ScreensCategories, Students, Timer, Playing, Stretching, Web landing page
Scope, stated plainly: the screens show meditation, a timer and stretching. They do not show appointments, records, prescriptions or clinical features, so this case study does not claim any.

The problem

Starting a calming practice is hard when you do not know which one fits. A stressed student and someone looking for focus need different sessions, and apps that bury them lose people before they begin.

Intended users

Likely users, not researched: students preparing for exams, people managing everyday stress, and beginners who want a short guided practice.

Needs

Find a relevant session fast, control time and sound, stay calm while using it, and know how long a session will take.

User journey in the screens

  1. Pick a category
  2. Choose a session (Students)
  3. Set music and timer
  4. Meditate
  5. Tap Done
  6. Stretch afterwards

Information architecture

Content is organised by the user’s need first (who it is for or how they feel), then by session. A bottom bar with four icons (home, meditation, progress, profile) keeps the main areas one tap away.

Visual system

Soft pink-to-mauve gradients, rounded imagery and circular category thumbnails make the app feel gentle. Bold sans headings and short labels keep the hierarchy clear. Calm photography on playing screens removes distraction.

Making information easier

Durations on cards, grouped timer settings and visible labels under every image reduce the guesswork before a session begins.

Accessibility and trust: retrospective

  • The bottom navigation uses icons without text labels; adding labels would help recognition and screen readers.
  • White text on photos (session cards) needs a stronger overlay to guarantee contrast.
  • The timer shows 07:11:13 while the session is 10 minutes; a clearer mm:ss format would avoid confusion.
  • The landing page shows percentage bars and health statements (for example about immunity). In a healthcare context these need credible sources, or softer wording, before release.
  • The glossy green Start and Pause buttons differ from the flat style elsewhere; aligning them would make the system more consistent.

Lessons learned

In a wellbeing product the interface should lower effort and never add pressure. Fewer choices per screen, clear durations and a quiet playing screen all serve that. I also learned that trust is built by careful claims as much as by visual polish.

Concept project · not implemented as a working app

Future You

“Visualize the person you want to become. Build the daily habits that help you get there.” A concept for connecting a desired future identity with everyday action.

TypeExploratory mobile app UI concept
StatusUI screens only. No functioning app, no user testing.
ScreensWelcome, Meet your future self, Home (two levels), Letter, Diary, Progress

The problem

People can picture the life they want, but staying consistent with small daily actions is where goals fade. Visualisation alone does not change behaviour.

The opportunity

Make the future self feel like a real, supportive person, then tie that picture to small actions, reflection and progress the user can see.

Intended users

Likely users, not researched: students, early-career professionals and anyone building habits around health, confidence, study or career.

Proposed journey and what the screens show

  1. Welcome and name
  2. Meet your future self (Level 1)
  3. Home: missions and reflection
  4. Read a letter from your future self
  5. Journal in the diary
  6. Track streak and levels

Daily reminders, goal selection and breaking a goal into steps are part of the intended experience but are not shown in these screens; they are proposed features.

Design decisions

A lavender-to-pink palette feels calm and aspirational. Cards, rounded corners and a four-tab bar (Home, Diary, Progress, Settings) keep a lot of content simple. The avatar and levels give a visible sense of movement toward a future identity.

How the pieces fit

Visualisation (avatar, letter) creates the picture; missions turn it into actions; the diary builds reflection; streaks and milestones show consistency. Reminders would connect these over time.

Encouraging, not shaming

Copy says things like “You’re exactly where you need to be right now” and “Progress isn’t always loud.” Missed days are met with acceptance. Mood tags include “Okay” as a valid state.

Inclusive design and retrospective critique

  • Several buttons are mid-grey with white text; they need stronger contrast and should not look disabled.
  • Emoji carry meaning in missions and moods; pair them with text and alt labels for assistive technology.
  • The progress screen shows 0 Total XP while Home shows 200 XP, a data inconsistency to fix in the prototype.
  • Gamified XP can reward points over meaning; consider letting users choose their own goals and pace.
  • Phrases such as “wiring my brain for success” should be softened so the app does not imply guaranteed results.

Proposed features (not designed yet)

  • Goal setup: choose an area such as health, confidence, study or career.
  • Breaking a goal into daily intentions the user edits.
  • Personalised, gentle reminders at times the user chooses.
  • Weekly reflections that suggest adjusting the plan.

What I learned

Designing a product around identity, not just tasks, changes the questions: tone matters as much as layout, and every motivating element needs a kind failure state. Without testing, I treat all of this as a hypothesis.

Design approach

This is how I like to work. It is my approach, not a claim that every project above included formal research or testing.

  1. UnderstandClarify the goal, the people and the constraints before opening a design tool.
  2. DefineName the core problem and the one job each screen must do.
  3. ExploreCompare layouts and flows quickly, keeping the simplest.
  4. DesignBuild hierarchy, type, colour and components into a consistent system.
  5. EvaluateReview for clarity, contrast and flow, then test with real users when possible.
  6. RefineFix what the review shows and note what to improve next.

About me

I studied B.Tech in Computer Science and Engineering at BML Munjal University and have worked on frontend and application development as well as interface design.

That mix means I think about a screen as both an experience and a build: how it adapts across screen sizes, what a developer needs to implement it, and where a design decision has a technical cost. I enjoy talking through those trade-offs early.

I’m early in my design career, and I’m looking for a team where I can learn from experienced designers while contributing thoughtful, user-centred work.
